proposals.name: Question-constraint alignment
proposals.rationale: Accepted answers must solve the asker’s actual, explicitly bounded problem.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer explicitly satisfies each stated requirement and limitation; low when it answers a nearby problem or silently violates constraints. Does not apply when no concrete constraints are stated.

proposals.name: Symptom-to-mechanism mapping
proposals.rationale: Mechanistic alignment helps the asker recognize whether the proposed fix addresses their failure.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer connects the reported symptom to a visible cause and corresponding remedy; low when it supplies an unexplained generic fix. Does not apply to purely non-diagnostic how-to questions.

proposals.name: Observable success check
proposals.rationale: Clear verification lets the asker confidently decide whether the problem is solved.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer provides an output, assertion, test, or other check showing how success can be recognized; low when success remains unverifiable. Does not apply when the answer is entirely conceptual.

proposals.name: Assumption visibility
proposals.rationale: Visible assumptions prevent apparently correct answers from failing in the asker’s context.
proposals.description: Scores high when required assumptions about inputs, state, or environment are stated; low when essential assumptions are hidden. Does not apply when the solution has no material assumptions.

proposals.name: Version-boundary clarity
proposals.rationale: Compatibility with the asker’s stated version can determine acceptance.
proposals.description: Scores high when version-sensitive behavior is explicitly bounded or qualified; low when version-dependent advice is presented as universal. Does not apply when the answer uses demonstrably version-independent constructs.

proposals.name: Localized adaptability
proposals.rationale: Adaptable answers are more likely to fit the asker’s unstated nearby needs.
proposals.description: Scores high when likely variations can be handled through clearly identified local edits; low when adapting the answer requires reconstructing an opaque solution. Does not apply to one-off outputs with no meaningful variation.

proposals.name: Failure-path explicitness
proposals.rationale: Handling foreseeable failure increases the chance the answer works beyond the happy path.
proposals.description: Scores high when relevant errors or unsuccessful inputs receive an explicit, understandable treatment; low when the main path is shown but predictable failure behavior is ignored. Does not apply when failure is outside the question’s scope.

proposals.name: Semantic side-effect disclosure
proposals.rationale: Hidden semantic changes can make an otherwise working answer unacceptable.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer identifies changes to ordering, mutation, persistence, precision, or other semantics; low when such changes are silently introduced. Does not apply when no meaningful side effects can occur.

proposals.name: Executable-context sufficiency
proposals.rationale: Sufficient context reduces implementation friction and ambiguity for the asker.
proposals.description: Scores high when executable code includes the essential setup, names, imports, and inputs needed to understand or run it; low when critical context is omitted. Does not apply to answers containing no executable code.

proposals.name: Dependency-cost proportionality
proposals.rationale: Acceptance depends partly on whether the remedy is practical in the asker’s environment.
proposals.description: Scores high when new dependencies are avoided or clearly justified by the problem’s complexity; low when an unexplained package adds installation or maintenance burden. Does not apply when no dependency choice is involved.

proposals.name: Alternative-selection rationale
proposals.rationale: Choosing among plausible solutions helps the asker act rather than merely browse options.
proposals.description: Scores high when multiple approaches are compared against identifiable constraints and one is recommended; low when alternatives are listed without guidance. Does not apply when only one approach is presented.

proposals.name: Output interpretation
proposals.rationale: Interpretation connects implementation details to the asker’s intended outcome.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer explains what its output means and how it satisfies the requested result; low when raw output is presented without interpretation. Does not apply when no output or result is produced.

proposals.name: Uncertainty separation
proposals.rationale: Calibrated confidence helps the asker judge whether further investigation is needed.
proposals.description: Scores high when confirmed observations, hypotheses, and suggestions are clearly distinguished; low when speculation is stated with unjustified certainty. Does not apply when the answer makes no diagnosis or uncertain claim.

proposals.name: Correction traceability
proposals.rationale: Transparent corrections preserve a clear decision path for the asker.
proposals.description: Scores high when a revision identifies the earlier claim, explains the change, and states which guidance now applies; low when conflicting advice is silently replaced. Does not apply to standalone answers.

proposals.name: Integration-path continuity
proposals.rationale: Answers that preserve the asker’s surrounding work are easier to adopt and accept.
proposals.description: Scores high when the proposed change fits the asker’s shown workflow and interfaces with localized modifications; low when it replaces that workflow without integration guidance. Does not apply when no existing workflow is provided.

proposals.name: Answer length
proposals.description: Count the answer’s overall words or paragraphs, ignoring code content.

proposals.name: Code-block density
proposals.description: Judge the proportion of the answer occupied by fenced or indented code, including repeated snippets.

proposals.name: Solved-claim wording
proposals.description: Mark explicit phrases such as “solved,” “worked,” “problem fixed,” or “this helps.”

proposals.name: External-link density
proposals.description: Count hyperlinks to documentation, gists, repositories, or other sites relative to answer length.

proposals.name: Documentation quotation
proposals.description: Mark quoted documentation, formal API descriptions, or phrases like “the docs say.”

proposals.name: Version specificity
proposals.description: Mark explicit Python, library, operating-system, or tool versions and dated compatibility references.

proposals.name: Addendum framing
proposals.description: Mark phrases such as “to add to,” “amend,” “another option,” or references to a preceding answer.

proposals.name: Boilerplate hedging
proposals.description: Mark recurring disclaimers or hedges such as “I think,” “not sure,” “in my case,” or “should work.”

proposals.name: Transcript evidence
proposals.description: Mark console prompts, stack traces, benchmark output, sample output, or other copied execution transcripts.

proposals.name: Library-name markers
proposals.parent: who answers the question and topic popularity
proposals.description: Mark answers dominated by recognizable package, framework, or platform names in prose or code.

proposals.name: Explicit Closure Signal
proposals.rationale: Resolved outcomes closely align with an asker’s decision to accept an answer.
proposals.description: High when the answer reports a successful resolution or concrete expected end state; low when it only proposes a possibility. Does not apply when no observable end state is relevant.

proposals.name: Error-to-Fix Traceability
proposals.rationale: Clear causal mapping helps askers recognize that their exact problem was solved.
proposals.description: High when the answer connects the stated symptom to a specific cause and corresponding change; low when code appears without that chain. Does not apply absent an error or symptom.

proposals.name: Setup Assumption Disclosure
proposals.rationale: Askers can accept solutions whose applicability conditions are explicit and satisfied.
proposals.description: High when required versions, inputs, state, or dependencies are stated or bounded; low when unstated prerequisites could change the result. Does not apply when no meaningful prerequisites exist.

proposals.name: Observed-Result Evidence
proposals.rationale: Concrete evidence increases confidence that the answer works in the asker’s situation.
proposals.description: High when the answer shows a test, output, or behavior produced by the proposed solution; low when it merely claims success. Does not apply to purely explanatory questions.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Discriminability
proposals.rationale: Discriminating diagnostics help askers verify they pursued the right resolution.
proposals.description: High when checks distinguish the proposed cause from plausible alternatives; low when troubleshooting advice cannot separate causes. Does not apply when only one cause is textually possible.

proposals.name: Constraint Conjunction Handling
proposals.rationale: Acceptance depends on solving the whole request, including interacting constraints.
proposals.description: High when multiple explicit requirements are satisfied simultaneously and their interaction is addressed; low when fixing one requirement violates another. Does not apply to single-requirement questions.

proposals.name: Semantic-Preserving Transformation
proposals.rationale: Askers accept transformations that retain the information they actually intended to preserve.
proposals.description: High when conversion or reshaping preserves intended meaning, ordering, units, or labels; low when only the representation changes. Does not apply when transformation semantics are immaterial.

proposals.name: State-Transition Awareness
proposals.rationale: Stateful mistakes often explain why seemingly correct answers fail for the asker.
proposals.description: High when required operation order, initialization, cleanup, or timing is handled; low when the answer assumes state already exists. Does not apply to stateless tasks.

proposals.name: Version-Boundary Precision
proposals.rationale: Version precision prevents askers from accepting fixes that cannot apply to their environment.
proposals.description: High when the answer identifies applicable versions or limits universal claims; low when version-specific advice is presented as timeless. Does not apply when version independence is explicit.

proposals.name: Alternative-Selection Guidance
proposals.rationale: Guidance tailored to the asker’s priorities is more likely to earn acceptance.
proposals.description: High when alternatives are compared against stated goals and recommended conditionally; low when options are listed without selection logic. Does not apply when no meaningful alternatives exist.

proposals.name: Minimal-Change Targeting
proposals.rationale: Askers favor fixes that solve their problem without imposing unrelated changes.
proposals.description: High when the modification is narrowly scoped and preserves unrelated behavior; low when broad replacement is offered unnecessarily. Does not apply to greenfield or full-rewrite requests.

proposals.name: Input-Output Contract
proposals.rationale: A visible contract lets askers judge whether the answer meets their practical objective.
proposals.description: High when expected inputs, outputs, and important side effects are explicit; low when successful use requires guessing them. Does not apply when no meaningful interface exists.

proposals.name: Revision Provenance
proposals.rationale: Explaining revisions helps askers trust an answer that resolves an observed failure.
proposals.description: High when an answer changing an earlier approach explains what was wrong and why the revision helps; low when it silently supersedes guidance. Does not apply when no earlier approach is referenced.

proposals.name: Scope-Risk Warning
proposals.rationale: Askers are more likely to accept solutions they can apply without unintended damage.
proposals.description: High when destructive, lossy, or global effects are flagged with safer boundaries; low when material risks remain implicit. Does not apply when no meaningful side effects exist.

proposals.name: Direct Applicability Mapping
proposals.rationale: Visible mapping reduces the effort required for an asker to recognize personal relevance.
proposals.description: High when each major step maps visibly to a named element, line, or requirement in the question; low when advice is generic. Does not apply to fully abstract questions.

proposals.name: RAW LENGTH
proposals.description: Character or token count of the answer | Longer answers may attract acceptance through visibility or perceived effort, independent of correctness.

proposals.name: CODE SHARE
proposals.description: Fraction of text inside code blocks | Answers dominated by runnable code may be favored over equally correct prose explanations.

proposals.name: LINK DENSITY
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: Number of URLs or citations | Documentation links can signal authority and attract acceptance regardless of whether the answer itself solves the problem.

proposals.name: UPDATE CUES
proposals.description: Phrases such as “updated,” “new answer,” or “since this question” | These phrases can identify late or follow-up answers whose acceptance depends on answer timing.

proposals.name: SOLUTION CLOSURE
proposals.description: Phrases such as “worked,” “solved,” or “finally” | Post hoc success language may mirror the asker’s interaction or voting behavior rather than answer quality.

proposals.name: VERSION MARKERS
proposals.description: Explicit version numbers or deprecated API names | Release timing can make certain answers more likely to be accepted because they match the asker’s environment.

proposals.name: TOPIC MARKERS
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: Named frameworks, libraries, or platforms | Certain technologies may have answerer and asker populations with systematically different acceptance habits.

proposals.name: QUESTION ECHO
proposals.description: Repetition of the question’s distinctive words or variables | Lexical mirroring can make an answer feel personally responsive and influence the asker’s verdict without adding technical merit.

proposals.name: TEMPLATE BOILERPLATE
proposals.description: Stock openings, disclaimers, or closings | Reusable answer templates may reflect cross-posting or author house style and predict acceptance independently of content.

proposals.name: COMPETING-ANSWER REFERENCES
proposals.description: Mentions of other answers, comments, or additions | References such as “to add to” or “alternative to” can signal bounty-driven or late competitive answering.

proposals.name: REQUIREMENT COVERAGE
proposals.rationale: Accepted answers must solve the asker’s actual request, including its explicit conditions.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer addresses every explicit subtask and stated constraint; low when it solves only a nearby problem. It does not apply when the question contains no distinct requirements.

proposals.name: CONTEXTUAL ADAPTATION
proposals.rationale: Tailoring signals that the answer is usable for the asker’s presented situation.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the solution uses the question’s actual objects, libraries, data shape, and environment; low when it substitutes an unrelated generic setup. It does not apply when the question provides no meaningful context.

proposals.name: CAUSAL DIAGNOSIS
proposals.rationale: Understanding the cause helps determine whether the proposed fix truly solves the problem.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer explains the mechanism causing the reported behavior and connects it to the remedy; low when it merely suggests a workaround. It does not apply to purely definitional or recipe questions.

proposals.name: VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
proposals.rationale: Evidence makes solution claims more trustworthy to the asker.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer shows a test, output, calculation, or other text-grounded check of the claimed result; low when success is only asserted. It does not apply when no observable result can reasonably be demonstrated.

proposals.name: BOUNDARY-CASE COVERAGE
proposals.rationale: Accepted solutions must remain useful across the asker’s likely inputs.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer handles edge cases suggested by the question or example; low when foreseeable boundary inputs silently break it. It does not apply when the task has no plausible edge cases.

proposals.name: SIDE-EFFECT SAFETY
proposals.rationale: Unexpected side effects can make an otherwise technically correct answer unusable.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when operations avoid unexplained mutation, deletion, global changes, or irreversible external effects; low when such effects are introduced silently. It does not apply to answers whose operations are purely observational.

proposals.name: FAILURE-MODE GUIDANCE
proposals.rationale: Practical recovery matters when the initial fix does not work immediately.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer identifies likely failure conditions and gives a response or diagnostic for them; low when failure leaves the user without direction. It does not apply when the operation has no meaningful failure mode.

proposals.name: DEPENDENCY TRANSPARENCY
proposals.rationale: Undisclosed dependencies can prevent the asker from applying the answer.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when required packages, tools, or services are named and their necessity is clear; low when dependencies are hidden or introduced without warning. It does not apply when the answer uses only built-in functionality already shown.

proposals.name: VERSION SENSITIVITY
proposals.rationale: Compatibility determines whether the answer works in the asker’s environment.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when version-specific behavior is identified and alternatives or limits are stated when relevant; low when brittle code is presented as universal. It does not apply when the answer uses version-stable constructs.

proposals.name: CODE-PROSE CONSISTENCY
proposals.rationale: Internal consistency prevents the asker from following contradictory instructions.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the explanation, names, inputs, and code behavior agree; low when prose promises something the snippet does not do. It does not apply when no code or procedural claim is offered.

proposals.name: EXECUTABLE PATH COMPLETENESS
proposals.rationale: A complete path reduces guesswork between reading and applying the answer.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the shown steps include the essential imports, definitions, inputs, and invocation needed to adapt or run them; low when key pieces are unexplained or omitted. It does not apply to answers intentionally limited to a single expression.

proposals.name: EXPECTED-EFFECT VISIBILITY
proposals.rationale: Clear success signals let the asker confirm resolution independently.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer states what successful application should produce or change; low when the user cannot tell whether it worked. It does not apply when the requested result is directly visible from the operation itself.

proposals.name: ALTERNATIVE TRADEOFF EXPLICITNESS
proposals.rationale: Choice guidance helps the asker select the answer that fits their constraints.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when multiple approaches are accompanied by concrete conditions or tradeoffs for choosing among them; low when alternatives are listed without guidance. It does not apply when only one approach is proposed.

proposals.name: SCOPE AND LIMIT PRECISION
proposals.rationale: Precise scope prevents false confidence that a partial fix solved the whole problem.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer distinguishes exactly what the proposed fix addresses from what it does not; low when it overclaims generality. It does not apply when the question is wholly narrow and unambiguous.

proposals.name: SEMANTIC INVARIANT PRESERVATION
proposals.rationale: Preserving meaning is essential for an answer to solve the underlying task.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when transformations preserve the real-world meaning of the data, not merely its shape or type; low when output is mechanically produced but semantically altered. It does not apply when the data has no stated interpretation.

proposals.name: Resolution self-report
proposals.description: Phrases such as “solved,” “worked,” or “problem fixed.”

proposals.name: Edit/update markers
proposals.description: Visible “update,” “edit,” “revised,” or appended follow-up sections.

proposals.name: Alternative-answer framing
proposals.description: Phrases such as “another option,” “to add,” or “based on the accepted answer.”

proposals.name: Authority-signaling references
proposals.description: Documentation citations, named experts, or repeated attribution to other users.

proposals.name: Cross-answer dependence
proposals.description: References to comments, other answers, gists, or material already presented elsewhere.

proposals.name: Gratitude and urgency boilerplate
proposals.description: Expressions such as “finally,” “thanks,” “please help urgently,” or “hope this helps.”

proposals.name: Niche topic fingerprint
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: Prominent framework, library, platform, or domain-specific vocabulary.

proposals.name: Version-era syntax
proposals.description: Explicit old versions, deprecated APIs, or historically distinctive Python syntax.

proposals.name: Code-to-prose ratio
proposals.description: The response is dominated by code blocks with very little explanation, or the reverse.

proposals.name: Markup-density style
proposals.description: Unusually heavy headings, blockquotes, horizontal rules, inline code, or formatting decoration.

proposals.name: Causal diagnosis with remedy
proposals.rationale: A convincing cause-and-fix chain helps the asker recognize that their particular problem was solved.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer links the reported symptom to a text-supported cause and gives a matching remedy; scores low when it merely substitutes a workaround or asserts a cause. Does not apply to purely instructional questions without a reported failure.

proposals.name: Explanation-code agreement
proposals.rationale: Consistency reduces the chance the asker follows a solution different from the one explained.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when prose, snippets, and outputs make consistent claims and use matching variables or APIs; scores low when they contradict one another. Does not apply when the answer contains no code or explanatory claim.

proposals.name: Explicit assumption visibility
proposals.rationale: Visible assumptions let the asker judge applicability before discovering hidden prerequisites.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when required inputs, versions, shapes, dependencies, or execution conditions are stated; scores low when applicability depends on silent assumptions. Does not apply when the question already supplies every relevant condition.

proposals.name: Text-only reproducibility
proposals.rationale: Self-contained instructions make successful verification possible without reconstructing missing context.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the method can be followed using material supplied in the answer or clearly defined substitutes; scores low when crucial files, data, or steps are omitted. Does not apply to answers addressing only a conceptual definition.

proposals.name: Compatibility boundary handling
proposals.rationale: Explicit boundaries prevent technically correct advice from failing in the asker’s environment.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer identifies relevant version, platform, or library boundaries and scopes its advice accordingly; scores low when context-sensitive code is presented universally. Does not apply when no compatibility-sensitive element appears.

proposals.name: Prompt-linked edge handling
proposals.rationale: Edge handling increases confidence that the answer solves the actual case, not merely a simplified one.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer handles boundary cases explicitly implied by the question; scores low when it works only on an unstated happy path. Does not apply when the prompt presents no meaningful edge case.

proposals.name: Input-output contract fidelity
proposals.rationale: Preserving the contract avoids solutions that run but produce unusable or altered results.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer preserves the requested type, shape, ordering, units, or semantics; scores low when it silently changes them. Does not apply when the question specifies no output contract.

proposals.name: State and lifecycle alignment
proposals.rationale: Correct timing matters because lifecycle errors can make otherwise valid code ineffective.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when operations occur at the correct stage of a loop, file, graph, request, or model lifecycle; scores low when valid operations are mistimed. Does not apply to stateless one-shot computations.

proposals.name: Failure containment without masking
proposals.rationale: Safe handling solves the immediate issue without concealing future failures or corrupting state.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when errors are prevented or handled while preserving useful visibility and state integrity; scores low when broad handling silently swallows failures. Does not apply when the answer involves no failure path.

proposals.name: Dependency cost proportionality
proposals.rationale: Proportionate dependencies reduce setup friction and support acceptance when simpler routes suffice.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when added dependencies are necessary, lightweight, or justified relative to the task; scores low when they impose unexplained setup burden. Does not apply when the solution uses no external dependency.

proposals.name: Diagnostic discriminability
proposals.rationale: Distinguishing diagnoses turns uncertainty into actionable progress toward the asker’s resolution.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when proposed checks or observations distinguish among plausible causes; scores low when advice relies on untestable speculation or undifferentiated trial and error. Does not apply when the fix is directly deterministic.

proposals.name: Alternative choice justification
proposals.rationale: Constraint-aware choice helps the asker select a method fitting their environment and objective.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when alternatives are compared against stated constraints and the selected method is justified; scores low when choices are listed or arbitrary. Does not apply when only one viable approach is presented.

proposals.name: Action order and stopping condition
proposals.rationale: Ordered steps and stopping criteria make advice operational rather than merely informative.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when instructions are sequenced and specify how to know the problem is resolved; scores low when order or completion criteria remain ambiguous. Does not apply to genuinely one-step answers.

proposals.name: Worked-result traceability
proposals.rationale: Traceable examples let the asker verify that results genuinely follow from the method.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when claimed outputs or examples demonstrably follow from the supplied code and inputs; scores low when results are generic or untraceable. Does not apply when no result is claimed.

proposals.name: Evidence-calibrated certainty
proposals.rationale: Calibrated certainty makes advice trustworthy when several plausible explanations remain.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when confidence matches the evidence in the answer and alternative interpretations are acknowledged; scores low when speculation is stated as fact. Does not apply when the text supports only one clear interpretation.

proposals.name: Long code blocks
proposals.description: The answer contains a large amount of code relative to prose, regardless of whether the code solves the stated problem.

proposals.name: External-link density
proposals.description: The answer relies on multiple hyperlinks or external references, measurable from the text alone.

proposals.name: First-person success claims
proposals.description: The answer says that the author tried something and it worked, solved the problem, or fixed the error.

proposals.name: Acceptance-like wording
proposals.description: The answer uses phrases such as “problem solved,” “this worked,” or “finally found the answer.”

proposals.name: Thank-you or credit language
proposals.description: The answer thanks named users, refers to comments, or credits another answer.

proposals.name: Version-specific syntax
proposals.description: The answer explicitly mentions a Python, framework, or library version, including obsolete or legacy versions.

proposals.name: Topic-specific library names
proposals.description: The answer contains recognizable names of niche frameworks, platforms, or specialized libraries.

proposals.name: Documentation-quote formatting
proposals.description: The answer reproduces a documentation statement in quotation or block-quote form before giving code.

proposals.name: Uncertainty disclaimers
proposals.description: The answer includes hedges such as “maybe,” “I guess,” “not sure,” or “should work.”

proposals.name: Generated-answer boilerplate
proposals.description: The answer uses stock phrases such as “here is an example,” “hope this helps,” or “for completeness.”

proposals.name: Self-answer reporting own resolution
proposals.rationale: Self-answers by the asker are typically self-accepted, decoupling acceptance from crowd-visible quality.
proposals.description: High if the answer is written in first person reporting what the author themselves did to fix their own problem ("I figured it out", "Turned out the problem was", "Solved it by"), rather than instructing a second party. Low if the answer addresses the reader in second person or is impersonal.

proposals.name: Announces resolution without explaining mechanism
proposals.rationale: Terse resolution announcements read as low articulated quality yet often mark accepted closure.
proposals.description: High if the text asserts the problem is solved ("problem solved", "and it worked", "no error now") but gives no causal account of why the fix works. Low if a mechanism, doc quote, or reasoning chain is supplied. Not applicable when no resolution is claimed.

proposals.name: Environment/installation fix versus code change
proposals.rationale: Install-level fixes are binary and immediately verifiable by the asker, driving acceptance regardless of elegance.
proposals.description: High if the operative remedy is a package install, reinstall, version pin, PATH/config change, or shell command rather than an edit to the asker's program logic. Low if the remedy is program code.

proposals.name: Explicit credit to a specific prior participant
proposals.rationale: Signals a resolved back-and-forth thread with the asker, which correlates with the asker closing it out.
proposals.description: High if the answer names a specific commenter/answerer (@handle or link to another answer) as the source or partial source of the solution. Low if no such attribution appears.

proposals.name: Positions itself as supplement to existing answer
proposals.rationale: Supplements arrive after acceptance is spent; they earn votes but not the asker's checkmark.
proposals.description: High if the answer opens by extending, correcting, or adding to another answer ("To add to X's answer", "I would amend the accepted answer", "Another option"). Low if it stands alone as a first-order response.

proposals.name: Solution scope matches the literal question
proposals.rationale: Askers accept what unblocks their stated problem, not the better-framed alternative.
proposals.description: High if the answer's target is exactly the artifact named in the question title, with no re-scoping. Low if the answer redirects to a different tool, different formulation, or answers an adjacent question. Not applicable if the question title is uninterpretable.

proposals.name: Verified output pasted from author's own run
proposals.rationale: Demonstrated execution converts a suggestion into a check the asker can confirm, aiding acceptance.
proposals.description: High if the answer includes console/REPL output, a printed result, or an image evidently produced by running the shown code. Low if only code is given with no execution evidence.

proposals.name: Diagnoses the asker's specific mistake
proposals.rationale: Targeted diagnosis directly resolves the asker's blocker; generic technique may be useful to others instead.
proposals.description: High if the answer points at a concrete error in the asker's posted code or setup ("you wrote data[key], change it to data2[key]", "your class name doesn't match the returned name"). Low if it presents a general technique without referencing the asker's artifact.

proposals.name: Hedged or speculative framing
proposals.rationale: Guesses invite comment threads rather than acceptance, even when substantively informative.
proposals.description: High if the answer contains explicit uncertainty about whether it solves the problem ("my guess is", "so I guess you can try", "not sure if", "it should work well enough", follow-up questions to the asker). Low if it asserts the fix confidently.

proposals.name: Performance benchmark as the contribution
proposals.rationale: Benchmark posts optimize an already-working solution; they attract votes but the asker is already unblocked.
proposals.description: High if the answer's main added value is timing comparison, %timeit output, or a speed claim against another posted approach. Low otherwise.

proposals.name: Answer is a bare one-liner remedy
proposals.rationale: Minimal fixes score poorly on articulated rubrics yet frequently are exactly what the asker needed.
proposals.description: High if the operative content is a single command or single expression with under roughly two sentences of surrounding prose. Low if there is structured explanation, multiple steps, or several code blocks.

proposals.name: Cites authoritative documentation or source code
proposals.rationale: Grounding is a genuine quality signal but is orthogonal to whether it unblocks this particular asker.
proposals.description: High if the answer quotes or links official docs, a library's source file, or a changelog to ground its claim. Low if assertions are ungrounded.

proposals.name: Tells asker why their approach cannot work
proposals.rationale: Negative answers resolve the asker's confusion but may leave them without a deliverable to accept.
proposals.description: High if the answer's core message is a constraint or impossibility ("you cannot change the function names", "it is wrong to resample that way") rather than an affirmative recipe. Low if it supplies a working construction.

proposals.name: Requires the asker to adopt a new dependency
proposals.rationale: New-dependency answers raise adoption cost for the asker while still being upvotable by others.
proposals.description: High if the recommended fix depends on installing a third-party library not already in the question. Low if the fix uses the standard library or libraries already present in the question.

proposals.name: Terse fix plus verified output, no explanation
proposals.rationale: Isolates the case where articulated rubrics penalize brevity but the asker has direct proof of resolution.
proposals.description: High only when both hold: the answer is short and mechanism-free AND it shows concrete evidence of working (pasted output, image, or "worked for me" with the exact command). Low if either half is missing. Composite of the terse-fix and verified-output criteria.

proposals.name: Self-answer resolution phrasing
proposals.parent: asker self-answering their own question, which they then accept
proposals.description: The answer is written in first person about the author's own problem being fixed ("I figured it out", "Got it!", "Problem solved", "after days of debugging"), rather than addressing a second-person "you". Judge by presence of first-person past-tense resolution language directed at the author's own situation.

proposals.name: Second-person instructional address
proposals.parent: third-party answerer competing with other answers
proposals.description: The answer is framed as advice to another person ("You can use...", "You need to...", "I would suggest you..."), with no first-person account of the author's own fix. Score on whether second-person pronouns dominate over first-person narrative.

proposals.name: Explicit reference to another answer
proposals.parent: answer order/timing — later arrivals after an answer is already accepted
proposals.description: The text cites, amends, corrects, or builds on another answer or answerer by name/link ("To add to Psidom's answer", "amend the accepted answer", "@X's answer might be incorrect"). Judge by any explicit mention of a competing or prior answer.

proposals.name: Thanks/credit to a commenter
proposals.description: The answer thanks or credits a named user or comment thread for leading to the solution ("Thank you @X for the discussion", "As per @CodeIt comments", "Follows from approach by @Andrew"). Judge by presence of gratitude or attribution to a specific person.

proposals.name: Very short prose-only fix report
proposals.parent: environment/installation-type questions with one true fix
proposals.description: Total answer under roughly 60 words with at most one short command or code line and no explanation of why it works (e.g. a single pip/conda install, one shell command, "problem solved"). Judge by word count plus absence of any explanatory clause.

proposals.name: Documentation-quote-and-link scaffolding
proposals.description: The answer's substance is a quotation from or link to official docs/source ("According to the README/docs...", blockquote of doc text, links into GitHub source lines) rather than author-written reasoning. Judge by whether removing the quoted/linked material leaves little content.

proposals.name: High markup density and section structure
proposals.parent: experienced high-rep answerers writing for crowd votes
proposals.description: The answer contains multiple distinct fenced code blocks, inline-code spans throughout, headers, bullet lists, and/or embedded images — heavy formatting relative to its length. Judge by counting formatting constructs (≥3 kinds present).

proposals.name: Benchmark or output-transcript padding
proposals.parent: crowd-vote-optimizing answerers on popular library questions
proposals.description: The answer includes timing comparisons (%timeit), REPL session transcripts with >>> prompts, or pasted result tables demonstrating correctness beyond the minimal fix. Judge by presence of measured performance numbers or interactive-session output.

proposals.name: Popular-library topic markers
proposals.parent: audience size determining how many answerers compete and whether the asker returns
proposals.description: The question/answer centers on a mass-audience library (pandas, numpy, regex, requests/BeautifulSoup) versus a niche or environment-specific topic (buildozer, Metaflow, rasa, GPG on Dataflow, driver/install errors). Judge from the library names and imports present in the text.

proposals.name: Alternative-among-many hedged framing
proposals.parent: late arrival to a question already answered
proposals.description: The answer presents itself as one option among several ("Another option", "An alternative answer is", "You could also", "a slight adjustment", "I know this is well-answered but") rather than as the solution. Judge by presence of alternative/additive framing in the opening sentence.

proposals.name: first-person resolution narrative
proposals.rationale: Matches asker-voice/relief framing common in self-accepted answers.
proposals.description: Answer frames itself as the asker's own solved-it story ("I solved it", "finally works", "problem solved") rather than neutral instruction to a third party; score high when this narrative voice is present, low when the answer is written as generic advice.

proposals.name: explicit addendum to another answer
proposals.rationale: Addenda are structurally unlikely to be the one the asker accepted.
proposals.description: Answer opens by referencing/building on another named or "accepted" answer ("to add to X's answer", "adding onto sascha's answer") rather than standing alone; score high when such framing appears, low otherwise; not applicable if no other answer is mentioned.

proposals.name: root-cause explanation vs fix-only
proposals.rationale: Root-cause clarity plausibly drives asker satisfaction beyond surface polish.
proposals.description: Score high if the answer states WHY the original code/approach failed (mechanism, misunderstanding) before or alongside the fix; score low if it only gives a replacement command/snippet with no causal explanation.

proposals.name: hedged or uncertain phrasing
proposals.rationale: Confidence signals may correlate with whether an asker trusted and accepted the fix.
proposals.description: Score high (present) when the answer uses hedges like "I think", "not sure", "probably", "might", "my guess is"; score low when phrased with confident, declarative statements.

proposals.name: mirrors asker's own exact code/variable names
proposals.rationale: Bespoke fixes tailored to the asker's literal code are strong accept signals.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer directly quotes or edits the asker's specific variable/function names or error text (e.g., "change data[key] to data2[key]") showing close reading of the question; low if answer is generic/library-level advice not tied to the asker's exact snippet.

proposals.name: single-command or one-liner fix
proposals.rationale: Terse fixes may be quickly verifiable and accepted, or conversely seen as low-effort.
proposals.description: Score high when the entire solution is one short command/line with minimal or no surrounding prose; score low when the answer is multi-paragraph or contains multiple code blocks/steps.

proposals.name: demonstrates verified working output
proposals.rationale: Shown proof-of-work plausibly increases asker confidence to accept.
proposals.description: Score high if the answer includes concrete output/result (console output, image, printed values) showing the fix actually ran successfully; score low if no evidence of execution is shown, only code.

proposals.name: critiques or corrects existing accepted answer
proposals.rationale: An answer positioning itself against the current accepted one is mechanically unlikely to itself be accepted.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer explicitly says a prior/accepted answer is wrong, incomplete, or "doesn't work for me" and offers a replacement; score low when it doesn't reference any other answer's correctness.

proposals.name: caveats or limitations disclosed
proposals.rationale: Honest caveats may build trust but could also signal an incomplete/unaccepted fix.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer notes conditions under which the fix might not work, trade-offs, or "your mileage may vary" type caveats; score low when presented as unconditionally correct.

proposals.name: installation/environment fix vs code fix
proposals.rationale: Environment-only fixes are a distinct resolution type that may pattern differently with acceptance.
proposals.description: Score high when the solution is a package reinstall/environment change (pip install, conda install, uninstall/reinstall) rather than a change to the asker's code logic; low when it's a code-level change.

proposals.name: tutorial-structured with headers/steps
proposals.rationale: Structured teaching format may signal thoroughness distinct from raw correctness.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer uses explicit structure like numbered steps, "Step 1:", markdown headers, or bulleted walkthroughs; score low for unstructured prose or bare code.

proposals.name: references external library not in question
proposals.rationale: Introducing new dependencies may lower practical acceptance despite technical merit.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer introduces a third-party package/library the asker's question did not mention as the core fix; score low when it stays within tools/libraries already implied by the question.

proposals.name: length disproportionate to question complexity
proposals.rationale: Over-elaboration relative to a simple ask may reduce likelihood of being the accepted, most-useful answer.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer's length/depth (multiple sub-sections, extensive background) seems clearly excessive relative to a simple, narrowly-scoped question; score low when answer length roughly matches question scope.

proposals.name: acknowledges/thanks a commenter or collaborator
proposals.rationale: Crediting help may correlate with genuine problem-solver (asker) authorship of the accepted answer.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer credits another user by name for helping reach the solution (e.g., "Thank you @X for the discussion"); score low when no such acknowledgment appears.

proposals.name: presents multiple alternative solutions
proposals.rationale: Multi-option answers may read as exploratory rather than the asker's own converged final fix.
proposals.description: Score high when the answer offers two or more distinct options/approaches (e.g., "Another option...", "if you are using X... however if Y...") rather than a single recommended fix; score low when only one solution path is given.

proposals.name: Solved-it framing phrase
proposals.description: Answer opens with first-person "solved it / figured it out / problem solved" narration rather than direct instructive prose.

proposals.name: Code-block-to-prose ratio
proposals.description: Proportion of the answer occupied by fenced code blocks versus explanatory prose; score high if mostly code, low if mostly text.

proposals.name: Hyperlink/citation density
proposals.parent: answerer's habit of referencing docs/source vs. writing standalone explanation
proposals.description: Count of embedded URLs, doc links, or "[see here]"-style citations per 100 words.

proposals.name: Reply-to-prior-answer markers
proposals.parent: answer posted late in thread, building on earlier posts
proposals.description: Answer explicitly references another answer ("as @X said", "adding to Y's answer", "the accepted answer") rather than standing alone.

proposals.name: Absolute answer length in characters
proposals.parent: answerer effort/verbosity habit and time invested
proposals.description: Raw character/word count of the answer body, independent of content quality.

proposals.name: Duplicate-question boilerplate
proposals.description: Same question title appears twice in the batch (near-duplicate cross-posted question), signaling a recurring/templated Q&A pair rather than unique content.

proposals.name: Terminal/REPL transcript formatting
proposals.description: Answer includes a pasted interactive shell/REPL session (">>>" prompts, command output) rather than a clean code snippet.

proposals.name: Package install one-liner pattern
proposals.description: Entire answer is essentially a pip/conda install or uninstall-reinstall command sequence with minimal explanation.

proposals.name: Thanks/acknowledgment sign-off
proposals.description: Answer ends with gratitude or credit to a commenter/other user ("Thank you @X", "Thanks to..."), signaling social exchange rather than pure content.

proposals.name: Numbered/bulleted step formatting
proposals.description: Answer uses explicit numbered lists, headers (####), or step labels ("Step 1:") versus a single flowing paragraph or code block.
